text: Leaf colour chart, feeding doses & natural plant protection for home and rooftop gardeners

Leihaao gives your plant a pH-balanced base with measured N, P and K, so feed extra only when the leaf colour chart says so. Look at your plant once a week, match a leaf to the chart, and follow the dose for that shade.

items: Check the soil first. Yellow leaves in wet, soggy soil usually mean overwatering, not hunger. Let the pot dry a little before feeding.
Always feed moist soil. Water lightly, then pour the fertiliser solution, so the roots do not burn.
Less is safer. If you are unsure between two shades, use the lower dose.
1 tsp = one level kitchen teaspoon (about 5 ml of liquid or 4–6 g of powder). Level it off with a knife.
All doses in this guide are per 1 litre of water. Dissolve fully and use the same day.
Water at room temperature works best. Rainwater or water stored overnight is ideal.

text: The Leihaao bag itself works as a large grow bag once you cut, fold and plant.
Leaf colour chart and NPK doses
Match your leaf to the chart below. Shades 1 to 3 need NPK, shades 4 and 5 need nothing, and shade 6 means you have overfed.
How to read the chart correctly

items: Pick the youngest fully opened leaf, usually the 3rd leaf from the top. Very new leaves are always lighter, and old bottom leaves are always darker.
Read in daylight, but in shade, with your back to the sun. Direct sunlight makes every leaf look lighter.
Hold the middle of the leaf flat against the chart. Do not compare the tip or the base.
Check 5 leaves from different plants or branches. Use the shade most of them match.
If a leaf falls between two shades, take the lighter shade's dose of the two, only if it is 3 or below.
Some varieties are naturally light green (lettuce, some basil) or naturally dark (curry leaf, spinach). Note your plant's colour when it is healthy and compare against that.

text: What to feed for each shade
Doses use a water-soluble NPK 19:19:19 fertiliser, dissolved in 1 litre of water. Pour the amount for your pot size from the table in the section above.

rows: Plant is starving, growth has stopped
Re-check after 2 feeds. If still pale, see the next section
At flowering and fruiting only, ¼ tsp once a month
Too much nitrogen. Soft growth, few flowers, attracts aphids
Flush the pot with plain water (twice the pot's volume) and wait 3–4 weeks

text: For fruiting plants (tomato, chilli, brinjal) that are at shade 4 or 5 but flowering poorly, a high-potash feed such as 13:0:45 at ½ tsp per litre every 15 days supports flowers and fruit.

Where a symptom starts on the plant points to its cause. Nutrients that can move inside the plant (N, P, K, Mg) leave the old leaves first. Nutrients that cannot move (Ca, S, Fe, Mn, Zn, B) show up on the new leaves first.

text: The 7-step plant check (5 minutes, once a week)

items: Look at the whole plant from 1 metre away. Is it upright or drooping? Is growth even or is one side weak? Note whether the problem is on one plant or all of them. If all plants in the same spot show it, suspect water, sun or heat first.
Push a finger 2 cm into the soil. Soggy soil with yellow leaves means overwatering. Dry, hard soil with limp leaves means underwatering. Fix watering before you feed.
Find where the symptom starts. Old bottom leaves, new top leaves, or scattered spots. Use the symptom finder above.
Read the pattern on the leaf.
Uniform yellow over the whole leaf: nutrient shortage (N or S).
Yellow between the veins, veins stay green: Mg on old leaves, Fe or Mn on new leaves.
Brown or burnt edges: K shortage, salt build-up from overfeeding, or sun scorch.
Spots with rings, fuzzy growth or powder: fungus.
Irregular light and dark green patches with crinkling: virus.
Turn the leaf over. Most insects hide on the underside and at stem joints. Use your phone camera's zoom as a magnifier.
Do the white paper tap test. Hold a white sheet under a branch and tap it. Tiny moving dots are aphids, mites or thrips.
Match a healthy-looking leaf to the leaf colour chart and note the shade, date and what you saw. Re-check the same plant in a week to see if it is getting better or worse.

rows: Whole leaf turns pale green then yellow, slow and thin growth. Leaf colour chart shade 1–3
Overwatering, natural ageing of 1–2 bottom leaves
Dull dark green with a purple or reddish tint on the underside and stems. Few flowers, weak roots
Cold nights, which also cause purpling
Yellow then brown, crispy leaf edges and tips. Fruits small or ripen unevenly
Salt burn from overfeeding, sun scorch
Yellow between the veins while veins stay green, like a Christmas-tree pattern. Sometimes reddish
Potassium shortage (Mg starts in the middle of the leaf, K at the edges)
New leaves curled or hooked with burnt tips. Black, sunken bottom on tomato and chilli fruit (blossom-end rot)
Uneven watering, which blocks calcium uptake
Whole young leaf evenly pale yellow, veins included
Nitrogen shortage (N starts on old leaves)
Bright yellow to almost white between veins, veins stay sharp green
Pale between veins with tiny brown dead spots, a checkered look
Iron shortage (Mn has spots, Fe does not)
Small, narrow leaves bunched at the tip (rosette), mottled yellow
Tip dies, new leaves thick and brittle, flowers drop, hollow or cracked stems
Rare. Young leaves limp, twisted, dark blue-green tips

text: If two or more symptoms show at once, the cause is usually the roots: overwatering, a root-bound pot or a pH problem. Correct that before adding any single nutrient.

Try the natural remedy first. Use the quick fix only if the symptom keeps spreading after 2 weeks. Organic remedies act slowly, so expect new healthy leaves in 10–20 days. Damaged leaves will not turn green again.

rows: Vermicompost tea: 2 tbsp vermicompost soaked in 1 litre water for 24 hours, strained. Or fermented rice water (rice washing water left 2–3 days), 1 cup in 1 litre
Soil drench every 7–10 days. Also mix 1 tbsp neem cake or mustard cake into the top soil once a month
NPK 19:19:19 as per the leaf colour chart
Bone meal, 1 tsp per medium pot. Or rock phosphate, 1 tsp per pot
Mix into the top 2–3 cm of soil and water in. Lasts 6–8 weeks
Banana peel tea: peels of 2–3 bananas soaked in 1 litre water for 2 days, strained. Or wood ash, ½ tsp per pot
Pour the tea as it is, every 10 days. Sprinkle ash on moist soil once a month only, since it raises pH
Epsom salt (magnesium sulphate), ½ tsp per litre
Spray on leaves or pour at the base, once every 2–3 weeks. Maximum 2 rounds
Same, but no more than 3 rounds in a season
Eggshell powder: dried eggshells ground fine, 1 tsp per pot. Faster: eggshell water (a handful of crushed shells soaked in 1 litre for 3 days), 1 cup per pot
Mix powder into top soil. Water evenly, never letting the pot dry out fully
Calcium nitrate, ¼ tsp per litre, as a spray
Gypsum, 1 tsp per medium pot. Epsom salt (above) also supplies sulphur
Mix into top soil once a season
First, stop overwatering and add 1 handful of compost to the top soil. Well-rotted compost releases iron slowly
Chelated iron (Fe-EDDHA), ¼ tsp per litre, as a drench once
Seaweed extract, ½ tsp per litre. Seaweed contains many trace nutrients
Spray on leaves every 15 days, 2–3 rounds
Zinc sulphate, ¼ tsp in 2 litres, one spray only
Compost and seaweed extract (above) usually cover it
Borax, a pinch (⅛ tsp) in 2 litres, one spray only. Boron turns toxic quickly, so never repeat within a month

items: Fermented buttermilk and jaggery tonic: 1 cup sour buttermilk + 1 tsp jaggery in 1 litre water, left overnight.
Use: pour 1 cup per pot every 15 days to feed soil microbes, which help release nutrients already in Leihaao.

text: Catch them early and a water jet or neem spray is enough. Both pests suck plant sap, multiply within days and are often farmed by ants.

rows: Tiny (1–3 mm), soft, pear-shaped. Green, black, yellow or brown. Some have wings
Small (3–5 mm), oval, covered in white cotton-like wax. Move slowly
Tender new shoots, flower buds, underside of young leaves
Stem joints, leaf bases, underside along veins, and roots near the soil surface
New leaves curl, crinkle and turn yellow. Growth becomes stunted
Leaves yellow, wilt and drop. Stems look dusted with white
Sticky shiny leaves (honeydew), black sooty mould, ants going up and down, white shed skins
White fluffy clumps, sticky honeydew, ants, black sooty mould. Plant wilts even when soil is moist (root mealybugs)
Rub the shoot with a finger. Aphids squash into a green or dark smear
Poke a white clump. It leaves a pinkish-red or orange smear

items: Check the underside of leaves and new shoots every week (step 5 of the plant check).
Do not overfeed nitrogen. Soft, blue-green (shade 6) growth attracts aphids.
Control ants. Ants protect these pests from their predators. Sprinkle cinnamon or turmeric powder around the pot base.
Keep new plants apart for 2 weeks before placing them with others.
Plant marigold, coriander, basil or mustard nearby. Their flowers attract ladybirds and lacewings, which eat aphids.
Hang yellow sticky traps (1 per 4–5 pots) to catch winged aphids.

rows: Every 2 days for a week, in the morning
Cotton bud dipped in rubbing alcohol (70% isopropyl)
Wipe each clump directly. Repeat after 3 days
1 tsp mild liquid soap (unscented, not detergent or dishwash with bleach)
1 tsp cold-pressed neem oil + ½ tsp liquid soap in warm water. Shake well
Both. Also stops eggs from hatching
Blend 10 garlic cloves + 2 green chillies in 1 cup water, soak overnight, strain, top up to 1 litre, add ½ tsp soap
1 tbsp neem cake soaked in 1 litre overnight, strained
Pour 1 cup per pot, every 10 days, 2 rounds

text: For a heavy mealybug attack, cut off the worst branches and put them in a sealed bag in the bin, then spray. Always spray both sides of the leaves and the stem joints.
Fungi spread through wet leaves, still air and wet soil, so dry leaves and good airflow prevent most of them. Remove infected leaves first, then spray.

rows: White or grey flour-like powder on the top of leaves. It rubs off with a finger
Older leaves first. Dry days with humid nights
Brown spots with rings like a target, often with a yellow halo. Spots join and the leaf dies
Lower leaves first, moving upward. Warm, wet weather
Yellow patches on top of the leaf with grey-purple fuzz underneath
Seedling stem turns thin, watery and brown at soil level, then the seedling falls over
Plant wilts and yellows even when soil is wet. Base of stem is dark and soft. Roots brown and smelly
Small orange-brown raised dots on the leaf underside. Rub off as rusty powder

text: If the spots have no rings, no fuzz and no powder, and new leaves are affected, check the nutrient table first.

items: Water the soil, not the leaves, and water in the morning so the surface dries by evening.
Space pots so leaves do not touch. Prune crowded inner branches.
Mulch the soil with dry leaves or straw so soil does not splash onto lower leaves.
Never reuse soil from a diseased plant, and clean scissors with alcohol between plants.
Add Trichoderma to the soil at planting: 1 tsp per medium pot mixed with a handful of compost.

rows: 1 tsp baking soda + ½ tsp liquid soap + 1 tsp vegetable oil
Powdery mildew. Spray on a sunny morning
Leaf spot, powdery and downy mildew
1 tsp neem oil + ½ tsp liquid soap
Pour 1 cup per pot every 15 days
Damping-off on seedlings, cut stems after pruning
Once, on the soil surface or cut

text: For blight or downy mildew that keeps spreading, a copper spray (copper oxychloride, ½ tsp per litre) is allowed in organic farming. Use it at most 2 times, 10 days apart.
A virus cannot be cured, in organic or chemical farming. You can only stop it spreading by removing sick plants and controlling the insects that carry it.

rows: New leaves small, thick, curled upward or downward, puckered. Plant bushy and stunted, few fruits
Irregular light and dark green or yellow patches like a jigsaw, leaves crinkled or twisted
Veins turn bright yellow in a net pattern, then whole leaf yellows. Fruits pale and hard

items: A virus pattern is uneven and patchy. Nutrient yellowing is even and repeats the same way on every affected leaf.
Virus-affected leaves are usually distorted (curled, crinkled, narrow). Nutrient-short leaves keep their normal shape.
Virus symptoms do not improve after feeding. If new leaves stay mottled 2 weeks after the right remedy, suspect a virus.
Look for the carriers: tiny white flies rising when you shake the plant, or aphids on the shoots.
Uproot the infected plant, put it in a sealed bag and bin it. Do not compost it or leave it in the garden.
Wash hands and clean tools with soap or alcohol after touching it. Avoid handling plants right after smoking, since tobacco can carry mosaic virus.
Control the carriers on the remaining plants: yellow sticky traps plus a neem oil spray (1 tsp per litre) every 7 days.
Remove weeds around the pots. They hide whitefly and aphids.
Buy healthy seedlings, and choose varieties labelled resistant to leaf curl or yellow vein mosaic where you can.
Do not replant the same crop in that pot for one season. Reuse the Leihaao medium for a different crop family instead.
Test any new spray on 2–3 leaves first and wait 24 hours. Skip it if leaves burn or spot.
Spray in the early morning or evening, never in hot midday sun.
Use one spray at a time. Do not mix soap, neem, baking soda and copper sprays together.
Wait at least 3 days after a neem or garlic spray before harvesting, and wash produce well.
Label every bottle, keep it away from children and pets, and wear gloves for copper, borax and alcohol.
Never go above the doses in this guide. More fertiliser burns roots faster than it helps.
